headline: Rhode Island departments win $4.54M in federal firefighter grants
dek: The awards will replace aging apparatus, upgrade breathing equipment and radios, and expand training in communities from Providence to Prudence Island.
body: Rhode Island fire departments and a statewide training academy will receive $4,538,706 in federal grants for equipment, vehicles and instruction, a package that officials say will improve both firefighter safety and emergency response across the state. The awards were announced by Rhode Island's congressional delegation and detailed in reporting by [Rhode Island Current](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/10/05/fema-awards-more-than-4-5m-to-rhode-island-fire-departments/).

Providence received the largest award, $1,849,284. The city plans to spend nearly $1.5 million on new self-contained breathing apparatus, commonly called Air-Paks, according to city information reported by Rhode Island Current. The remaining money will support nationally standardized supervisory training for lieutenants, captains and chief officers. The department expects to buy the breathing equipment within the next few months and put it into service in early 2027; it has two years to spend the award after accepting it.

The grants also target apparatus that can determine how quickly a department reaches a fire or medical call. Woonsocket will receive $1 million for a new aerial ladder truck to replace an obsolete vehicle that has become difficult and expensive to repair. Coventry will receive $499,177 for an ambulance to replace a Central Coventry Fire District vehicle with more than 250,000 miles, the delegation's [official announcement](https://www.whitehouse.senate.gov/news/release/ri-delegation-delivers-nearly-4-5-million-for-local-firefighters/) said.

Other awards are smaller but address specific gaps. West Warwick will use $339,932 to update hose and nozzle equipment on a frontline engine and buy two cardiac monitors. The Prudence Island Volunteer Fire Department will receive $255,015 for 34 portable radios. In Lincoln, Lime Rock Fire Department will get $99,840 for cardiac monitor-defibrillators, while Quinnville Fire District will get $57,191 for four portable radios and a thermal-imaging camera. Newport will receive $68,181 for three Lucas mechanical CPR devices.

The Rhode Island Fire Training Academy will receive $370,086 for a fire-truck simulator, three forcible-entry doors, 15 self-contained breathing apparatuses and 40 reflective helmet covers. The simulator and practice equipment are intended for training rather than frontline deployment, but they matter to departments that need recruits and current firefighters to practice high-risk operations in a controlled setting. The award also gives the academy equipment that can be used by firefighters from multiple communities rather than a single department.

The money comes through the federal Assistance to Firefighters Grant program. The [U.S. Fire Administration](https://www.usfa.fema.gov/a-z/grants/) says the program supports eligible career and volunteer departments, emergency medical organizations and state fire-training academies with equipment, training, firefighter health and safety initiatives, and efforts to maintain a trained frontline workforce. The grants are competitive: the Rhode Island delegation said awards are evaluated based on need, project scope, community impact and application merit.

The statewide announcement combines awards that FEMA released separately in late September and early October. That timing explains why the grant package includes a mix of purchases rather than one coordinated state project. Providence's planned Air-Paks and Woonsocket's ladder truck address the most visible equipment needs, while radios, cardiac monitors and thermal-imaging equipment can improve communication, patient care and scene awareness in smaller departments and volunteer organizations.

The awards do not immediately put new vehicles or equipment into service. Departments must accept the grants, complete purchasing and follow the program's performance requirements. Providence has supplied the clearest schedule so far, with new breathing equipment expected early next year; the other communities' delivery dates were not announced in the sources reviewed for this report. The practical impact will depend on how quickly each recipient can complete procurement and training.

The congressional announcement said Rhode Island fire departments and other first responders have received more than $43 million through FEMA's Assistance to Firefighters, Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response, and Fire Prevention and Safety programs over the last three years. It also said the current round was supported by $648 million in fiscal 2025 federal funding for competitive fire grants nationwide. For Rhode Island residents, the new awards translate that national program into more specific local changes: safer breathing gear in Providence, a replacement ladder truck in Woonsocket, a high-mileage ambulance replacement in Coventry and updated communications and medical tools across the state.
